name: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking
problem: Dense retrievers lose the exact-match and interpretability properties of bag-of-words, while learned sparse retrievers had not matched their effectiveness.
mechanism: A learned sparse first-stage ranker: an MLM-style encoder whose output layer produces term weights, trained end to end with EXPLICIT SPARSITY REGULARISATION and a log-saturation effect on weights, so representations are highly sparse and inherit inverted-index efficiency. Term weights are a learned version of BM25 expansion - they encode both importance and document frequency effects.
speedup_reported: Competitive with state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods while trained end to end in a single stage; the paper also explicitly studies the effectiveness/efficiency trade-off by varying the sparsity-regularisation weight. Baselines named, but no absolute latency or hardware throughput figures.
notes: Venue SIGIR 2021 short paper (ACM DOI 10.1145/3404835.3463031; arXiv comment '5 pages, SIGIR'21 short paper'). WHY IT MATTERS FOR INFERENCE COST: a sparse embedding is a few hundred non-zero term weights rather than a dense 768/1024-dim vector, so the first-stage scan moves far fewer bytes and can run on an inverted index or a CPU - the SPLADE-MLP variant does exactly that. It is also the mechanism behind the sparse head of M3-Embedding (pap-mm-bge-m3), which serves both retrieval functions from one checkpoint. First-stage-only use is the normal deployment: sparse retrieval then dense/late-interaction rerank.
